summary: P.A.C.E. is a software prototype that helps an astronaut with sepsis who is far from Earth. It focuses on one hazard, distance from Earth, and mainly on the gap caused by delayed flight surgeon responses: a message to the ground can take up to 24 minutes one way, and the astronaut has no trusted guidance in the meantime. P.A.C.E. reads blood pressure, lactate and white blood cell count, rates them Normal, Needs attention or Urgent, shows the astronaut what to do next straight away, and sends the results to the flight surgeon. It matters because this gap can cost a lot without the astronaut knowing what to do.
details:
P.A.C.E. is an interactive prototype of a monitor screen for a crew member with sepsis, inside a spacecraft far from Earth.

How it works. Blood pressure comes automatically from the monitor (the CSA Bio-Monitor already measures it). Lactate and white blood cell count come from the astronaut’s blood test and are passed to the monitor; this link is my assumption, since no source confirms blood analyzers can send results to a monitor. P.A.C.E. checks each value against a range, and the worst value sets the overall level. Where NASA has a line, I used it (lactate above 2 mmol/L and mean arterial pressure below 65 mmHg are NASA’s septic-shock lines). Other ranges come from published medical sources, and the middle “Needs attention” band is my assumption.

What the astronaut sees. Normal: no action is needed, and values are shown only on request. Needs attention: the flight surgeon is gently informed, and next steps come first, with an example floor plan showing where supplies are. Urgent: results are sent to the flight surgeon and the astronaut is told; Check, Monitor and Treat steps from the sources appear; a timeline shows the delay (results sent, message reaches the ground, reply travels back); the reply button activates only when the last step completes, then opens the flight surgeon’s response as text with a Listen button.

Voice help. Every screen has a Listen button. If the astronaut does not understand, “No” opens a full-screen microphone; they speak, get an answer as text, and can listen to it.

Benefits and goals. Immediate guidance during the delay, less reading under stress, and an honest view of how long the reply will take.

Limits. All numbers are example data and P.A.C.E. is not a medical device. No source was found linking a spaceflight hazard to changes in the lactate or white blood cell values, and the treatment steps in the sources are written for trained providers.

Tools. Designed in Figma; built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript (browser speech features for Listen and voice input); fonts Inter, Public Sans and DM Mono; hosted on Netlify.
